title: The Bark That Crossed Oceans
paras: In seventeenth-century [[colonial|colonial]] Peru, where mule trains carried silver [[ore|ore]] towards distant ports, another valuable material entered European trade: cinchona bark. Derived from Andean trees, it acquired a reputation for relieving intermittent fevers. Although its early history remains contested, Indigenous knowledge was crucial to the encounter between this forest resource and European medicine, which gradually transformed bark into an international commodity.

Collectors removed strips that might [[encircle|encircle]] a trunk, sometimes killing the tree in the process. A botanical [[specimen|specimen]] could help identify a promising species, but appearance alone could not establish medicinal strength. Patients might [[terminate|terminate]] treatment because the preparation tasted intensely bitter; those caring for them could offer reassurance, yet words alone could scarcely [[console|console]] families after repeated bouts of fever.

In 1820, French chemists isolated quinine, making more consistent dosing possible. Later, European powers transferred cinchona seeds and plants to Asian plantations, hoping to [[reap|reap]] the benefits of controlled cultivation. Java eventually became a major supplier. Behind this achievement lay a frequently [[ruthless|ruthless]] commercial logic: control over plants, labour and distribution could be as valuable as the chemical knowledge itself.

Turning a plantation crop into accessible medicine nevertheless required more than abundant harvests. Transport costs and [[taxation|taxation]] influenced prices, while purchases could remain [[pending|pending]] until hospitals secured funds. Quinine never made malaria a simple problem, and synthetic medicines eventually reduced its dominance. Yet its history established a durable lesson: discovering an effective substance and ensuring that patients receive it are separate achievements.
zh: 在十七世纪受殖民统治的秘鲁，骡队将银矿石运往遥远的港口之际，另一种珍贵材料也进入了欧洲贸易网络：金鸡纳树皮。这种取自安第斯山脉树木的材料，因能够缓解间歇性发热而逐渐闻名。尽管其早期历史仍有争议，原住民知识在这种森林资源与欧洲医学的相遇中发挥了关键作用，而这一过程也逐渐使树皮成为国际商品。
采集者剥取的长条树皮可能绕树干一整圈，有时会因此导致树木死亡。植物标本可以帮助辨认具有药用潜力的物种，但仅凭外观无法确定药效强弱。由于药剂味道极苦，患者可能会中止治疗；照料他们的人虽然可以给予鼓励，但在一次次发热之后，单靠言语几乎无法慰藉家属。
1820年，法国化学家分离出了奎宁，使药物剂量能够更加稳定。此后，欧洲列强将金鸡纳树的种子和植株转移到亚洲种植园，希望从可控栽培中获益。爪哇最终成为主要供应地。这一成就背后，是一种往往冷酷无情的商业逻辑：对植株、劳动力和销售渠道的控制，可以与化学知识本身同样有价值。
然而，要把种植园作物转化为患者能够获得的药品，仅有丰收还不够。运输成本和税收影响着价格，而采购事宜可能要等医院筹得资金后才能确定。奎宁从未让疟疾变成一个简单的问题，后来出现的合成药物也逐步削弱了它的主导地位。不过，它的历史留下了一条长久适用的启示：发现有效物质与确保患者用得上它，是两项不同的成就。

q.s: Indigenous expertise played an important part in introducing cinchona to European medicine.
q.why: 第一段指出原住民知识发挥了关键作用。

q.s: Collectors could determine the medicinal potency of cinchona simply by examining its appearance.
q.why: 第二段明确说仅凭外观无法确定药效。

q.s: Hospitals in Java received financial priority over European hospitals when purchasing quinine.
q.why: 文中未比较两地医院采购资金的优先级。
